Policy "Parameterized SQL only":
SQL must be built with parameters or an ORM, never by concatenating or formatting strings with values that come from outside the program. Table and column names taken from constants in the code are fine.

File: app/users.py
Lines: 29-29
Rule message: Possible violation of the policy "Parameterized SQL only".

Code (flagged lines marked >>):

       2 | import sqlite3

       5 | USERS_TABLE = "users"
       6 |

      10 |

     ... |

      23 |     cur.execute(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {USERS_TABLE}")
      24 |     return cur.fetchone()[0]
      25 |

      27 | def rename_user(user_id, new_name):
      28 |     cur = get_connection().cursor()
>>    29 |     cur.execute("UPDATE users SET name = '%s' WHERE id = %s" % (new_name, user_id))
      30 |     log.info("renamed user %s", user_id)
</untrusted_code>

Why the reviewer kept it: Line 29 builds the UPDATE statement with Python's % operator, interpolating `new_name` and `user_id` directly into the SQL. These are function parameters that are not constants and can carry external input, so this is string-formatted SQL where a parameterized query was required.

WHERE id = ?\", (new_name, user_id))", "fix_note": "The `sqlite3` driver uses `?` placeholders, so the values are passed as a tuple and the file's existing `cur` cursor is reused."}
